newsitem.title: UK: British government bond market bets on Labour win.
newsitem.headline: British government bond market bets on Labour win.

text.p: A wary British government bond (gilt) market has already factored in an election victory by the opposition Labour Party and is even regarding the prospect with equanimity, analysts say.
"The market is a lot more comfortable with the idea of Labour in power than it used to be, partly because of the convergence of Labour and Conservative policies," HSBC economist Philip Tyson said.
In the past, the merest whisper that Labour might take power was enough to send gilt prices plummeting amid terror of a flood of bond issues to pay for expensive spending promises.

But Prime Minister John Major's announcement on Monday that the election will take place on May 1 cost gilts only 1/2 a point, in what dealers said was a knee-jerk reaction to long-awaited news rather than anxiety about Labour's policies.
For financial markets, the word "Labour" used to conjure up 1970s memories of a debt-laden Britain being bailed out by the International Monetary Fund, soaring inflation and punitive tax rates.
But under Tony Blair, Labour has been reborn.

It has committed itself to keeping within the ruling Conservative government's tight spending plans for the next two years, leaving income tax rates unchanged for the first term and meeting the official inflation target of 2.5 percent or less.
"In the last election, people thought a Labour government would borrow considerably more than a Conservative one but that's not the case now," said SBC Warburg economist Mark Reckless.
At the last British general election, in April 1992, opinion polls predicted either a narrow Labour victory or a hung parliament.
But once it became clear that the Conservatives had retained power, the gilt market errupted into euphoria.

Gilt prices rocketed four full points and the Bank of England used the burst of enthusiasm to sell 800 million stg of gilts in an unprecendented out-of-hours operation at 0234 in the morning. Part of the offering was so popular that dealers snapped it up almost as soon as it appeared on their screens -- the so-called "two minute tap."

The Bank has since adopted a fixed schedule for gilt issuance, leaving little scope for such opportunistic funding, although it might still be inclined to step in with additional supply if price rises look too wild.

Moreover, Labour's whopping opinion poll lead over the Conservatives means gilt prices have been steadily adapting to the idea of a Labour victory and the Labour-phobia which prompted massive gains on the 1992 vote result has evaporated.
In fact, analysts say the worst possible outcome for the gilt market would be no overall majority for either of the two main political parties.

"If you get a hung parliament there will be worries that another general election is imminent and that both monetary and fiscal policy would be looser than they ought to be," Goldman Sachs UK economist David Walton said.
An inconclusive election result would mean that both the major parties would concentrate on trying to win over voters rather than making potentially unpopular decisions on interest rates or taxes.
Whichever party is in power is likely to have to put up interest rates.

But Labour is likely to move faster than the Conservatives as it tries to establish tough anti-inflation credentials and analysts expect a 25 basis point increase in Britain's 6.0 percent interest rates soon after the election.
This would have the added benefit of ending the current disagreement between the Bank of England and the Treasury on the need for higher rates.
"If Labour were to win, I don't think Gordon Brown would want the dispute with the Bank of England to continue," Walton said, referring to Labour's shadow finance minister.
But the market's old worries about Labour might be reignited if the party swept to power with a massive majority in the House of Commons.
"The market doesn't know what it thinks of a big Labour majority," SBC Warburg's Reckless said. "A lot over 100 would be negative but then so would less than 20 or 30."
The market is concerned that a large majority might mean a higher proportion of left-wing members of parliament who could press for bigger spending pledges.
But a small majority might also be dangerous because potential rebels might hold a Blair government to ransom just as the anti-European faction has dealt with Conservative Prime Minister John Major.
